Subject: Post-call: SLO targets, measurement defs, and reproducibility next steps

Thanks again for carving out time today — helpful conversation. This thread is a short recap + concrete next steps so we have a single place to track measurement scope and the reproducibility checklist. TL;DR: Redwood can run a scoped qualification (3-day pilot) or hand over the harness for Traderly to run; below are the specific measurement defs we discussed and what we'll attach.

Summary of what we captured on the call:
- Latency SLOs: p95 <= 250ms for 512-token responses, p99 <= 600ms (streaming tolerance discussed below).
- Throughput goals: baseline 80 requests/s steady state at concurrency 32 for the standard checkout flow.
- Streaming: support chunked token emission with max delay per chunk <= 50ms; streaming reconnections should preserve KV cache where possible.
- Repro: canonical prompt set + deterministic evaluation harness; we recommend running with the same RNG seed, identical tokenization, and warm-up window (200 requests) before sampling.

Attachments I'm adding to the Drive link (also attached here as stubs): traderly_prompt_set_v1.jsonl (30 canonical prompts), slo_measurement_spec_v0.2.md (measurement definitions + supported tolerances), harness-integration-checklist.md (how to integrate Redwood harness), sample-results-latency.csv (example output).

Options & ask from Traderly:
1) Pilot run by Redwood (recommended if you want fast initial data): 3 days, we provide infra and run the harness with your prompt set, share raw traces (latency percentiles, concurrency profile, streaming chunk timing) and the canonical artifacts.
2) Self-run: we hand over harness + checklist; Traderly runs in your environment and we co-review the artifacts.

Please confirm which option you'd prefer and share: (a) the model variant you want to qualify (open model name + quantization if any), and (b) if you require private VPC-only runs for the pilot.

Next internal step: Ben will outline the measurement spec concretely and list the exact inputs we need from your side (sample payloads, auth access for sections of the harness if you choose pilot).

Thanks,
Irene
Irene Choi
Account Executive, Redwood Inference

Thanks Irene — quick clarifying Qs from our side after reviewing the recapped SLOs: 

1) Latency baseline: are the p95/p99 targets interpreted as end-user token emission (i.e., including streaming overhead) or server-side generation latency (time-to-first-byte + generation)? We need the number that maps to perceived UI latency.
2) Throughput: our checkout flow mixes short prompts (~40 tokens) and long completion (~600 tokens). For qualification should we run separate profiles (short/long) or a weighted mixed workload?
3) Repro: If we run the harness in our environment, what exact runtime/container image do you require? Also confirm the warm-up window size and whether KV cache persistence across reconnects is required.

We lean toward Redwood doing the pilot so we can get an apples-to-apples read, but we want to lock the measurement definitions first. We can also provide a small anonymized sample of real traffic (5k events) if that's useful for shaping the workload.

—Raj

Subject: Re: Post-call: SLO targets, measurement defs, and reproducibility next steps

Hi all — Ben (performance lead) here. Short answers and an attached minimal measurement spec (slo_measurement_spec_v0.2.md). I also dropped a short harness checklist in the Drive folder. Key clarifications below.

1) Latency measurement: we will report both server-side generation latency (time from request accept to last token emitted) and perceived UI latency (time-to-first-byte + first chunk emission). For your SLOs, we should target p95 perceived latency <= 250ms for the 512-token "standard" response profile; p99 covers tail behavior including network variance. When we say "streaming chunk delay <= 50ms" we mean between consecutive chunk emissions once streaming has started — not including time-to-first-byte.

2) Workload mix: please provide a weighted sample; if not available, we'll run two canonical passes + a combined mixed pass. Canonical passes: (A) short-response pass (40 tokens target) and (B) long-response pass (512–600 tokens). The mixed pass will use our default checkout mix: 60% short / 40% long unless you give different weights.

3) Cold vs warm: all measured numbers will be reported both cold-start (after a 30m idle window and fresh process) and warm-state (after a 200-request warmup window). Warm-state is what production should expect once caches and kernels are hot.

4) Determinism & RNG: the harness uses a fixed RNG seed by default and consistent tokenization (we pin to tokenizer v14 in the harness). Sampling parameters (temp/topk) will be reproduced exactly when you provide them in the prompt metadata. For non-deterministic sampling we report variance across N=5 runs.

5) KV cache + reconnects: our pilot preserves KV cache per-session when the client reconnects within the same session ID. If Traderly needs cross-session persistence we can simulate it but we'll need the session-id mapping and expected TTL.

6) Repro artifacts we will deliver (if Redwood runs pilot): raw traces (per-request latencies, per-chunk timings), token counts, concurrency traces (threads/CPU/GPU metrics), and a run manifest with harness version, docker image, and seed. The harness image we use: redwood/harness:0.9.1 and inference runtime tag: inference-runtime:1.4.

Files attached to Drive (and stubbed here): slo_measurement_spec_v0.2.md, harness-integration-checklist.md, sample-results-latency.csv, traderly_prompt_set_v1.jsonl. I annotated the prompt set with expected output lengths and any special placeholders (e.g., {{cart_items}}).

Next-step proposal: if Traderly wants Redwood to run the pilot, we can schedule a 3-day window starting as soon as next Tue (2026-10-13). We'll need model variant + quantization flag by EOD Mon (2026-10-12) and a short IP allowlist if you want VPC-only connectivity.

Happy to hop on a quick 20-min sync if you'd prefer to walk the measurement spec together.

—Ben
Ben Carter
Principal Performance Engineer, Redwood Inference
